newsitem.title: INDONESIA: East Timor crowd stones local parliament.
newsitem.headline: East Timor crowd stones local parliament.

text.p: A crowd of East Timorese angered by Indonesian attacks on Nobel Peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo stoned the territory's local legislature in Dili on Wednesday, an official said.
"The situation is a bit out of control. They are stoning the house of representatives," an official at the University of East Timor told Reuters by telephone.
Witnesses contacted in Dili said several hundred police in riot gear had blocked off streets and armed troops appeared to be preparing to deploy as demonstrators chanted anti- Indonesian slogans.
"We are against the Indonesian presence in East Timor and we are protesting against the criticism of Bishop Belo," one demonstrator was quoted as saying.
Police in Dili said only the police chief for the Dili district could comment and he was not immediately available.
The vice-rector at the University of East Timor, Armindo Maia, told Reuters he was trying to contain the situation at the university where more than 1,000 students had earlier started a protest.
He said about 1,000 university students had been joined by hundreds of high school students gathered on the road outside the campus in central Dili.

The protests came a day after the fifth anniversary of the shooting by troops of at least 50 demonstrators on their way to the Santa Cruz cemetery in Dili following the funeral of an anti-Indonesian activist killed two weeks earlier.
The university had closed on Tuesday, but reopened on Wednesday with students expected to write mid-semester examinations.
"But evidently it is a bit difficult," Maia commented wryly.

The latest demonstrations appeared to have been sparked largely by strong criticism and protests in Jakarta against Belo, probably the most powerful and highly-regarded civilian in mainly-Catholic East Timor.

Television footage seen in Dili on Tuesday night showed a demonstration in Jakarta by more than 2,000 members of youth groups allied to the country's ruling Golkar party who demanded the expulsion of Belo from the country.

The attacks on Belo follow an interview published in the German news magazine Der Spiegel in which he was reported as saying Indonesian troops had trampled on East Timor's independence "and treated us like dogs".
Belo, who flew to Jakarta on Monday for an annual meeting of Catholic bishops, has declined to comment until he sees the full text of the interview.
Indonesian troops invaded the former Portuguese colony in December 1975 and Jakarta declared it Indonesia's 27th province the following July in a move not recognised by the United Nations.
Four East Timorese men entered the Spanish embassy in Jakarta on Tuesday seeking political asylum.
